**Instructions.** Complete this assignment in Quarto or R Markdown and upload
both your `.qmd` source and the rendered `.html` to Brightspace. Show your code. Interpretation questions are
graded on precision (adjusted for what, units, association vs causation,
population), exactly as practiced in the labs. End with your AI-use statement
(see Section 4). This homework is a miniature of your project pipeline: EDA,
model selection, diagnostics, and honest reporting on one dataset.

**Data.** Body fat measurements for 252 adult men. The outcome is `brozek`,
percent body fat from Brozek's equation, computed from an underwater body
density measurement that is accurate but expensive; the goal is to predict it
from cheap body measurements. The dataset also contains `siri`, `density`,
and `free`, which are alternative versions of the outcome (Siri's equation,
the raw density, and fat-free weight); using them as predictors would be
cheating, so we drop them at the start.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
data(fat, package = "faraway")
body <- fat |>
  select(brozek, age, weight, height, neck, chest, abdom, hip, thigh)
```

Candidate predictors: `age` (years), `weight` (pounds), `height` (inches),
and circumferences in cm of `neck`, `chest`, `abdom` (abdomen), `hip`, and
`thigh`.

# Section 1: Do (6 points)

**1.1** EDA: numerical summaries of all nine variables and a histogram of
`brozek`. Report anything implausible you find in the predictor summaries
(look carefully at the minimum of `height`, and identify which row it belongs
to). (2 pts)

**1.2** Starting from the full model `brozek ~ .` on `body`, run backward
selection twice with `step()`: once with the AIC penalty (the default,
`k = 2`) and once with the BIC penalty (`k = log(n)`). Report the two
selected predictor sets and each model's R-squared. (2 pts)

**1.3** For the AIC-selected model: make the residuals-versus-fitted plot and
the Q-Q plot of residuals, then compute Cook's distances and leverages
(`hatvalues`). Report the case numbers with the largest Cook's distance and
(for the full eight-predictor model) the largest leverage, together with
those men's `weight` and `height`. (2 pts)

# Section 2: Interpret (8 points; interpretation precision counts double)

**2.1** AIC kept five predictors; BIC kept two. Which model would you carry
forward for the stated goal of cheap prediction of body fat, and why? Your
defense should mention what the two criteria reward differently and compare
the models' R-squared values. (2 pts)

**2.2** A classmate reports the p-values from the summary of the selected
model as if they were ordinary p-values. Explain in two or three sentences
why p-values computed on the same data that chose the model are optimistic
(too small), and what this means for how you should describe the selected
model's "significant" predictors. (2 pts)

**2.3** Consider the two cases you flagged in 1.3: the highest-leverage case
(the 29.5-inch height) and the highest-Cook's-distance case (the heaviest
man). For the height case, compute the BMI its recorded weight and height
imply. What should you do with each case, and on what grounds? Note that high
leverage with small Cook's distance and high influence call for different
reasoning. (2 pts)

**2.4** Write the strong-form interpretation of the `abdom` coefficient in
the BIC-selected model. Then explain in one sentence why the `weight`
coefficient in that model is negative even though heavier men have more body
fat overall (marginal correlation between `weight` and `brozek` is strongly
positive). (2 pts)

# Section 3: Critique the AI (6 points)

A student gave this dataset to an AI assistant and asked it to select and
report a model. The assistant replied:

> "Starting from the eight candidates (R-squared 0.79), backward stepwise AIC
> identified the true model: `brozek ~ weight + neck + abdom + hip + thigh`.
> BIC selected only `weight` and `abdom`, but the AIC model is better because
> its R-squared is higher (0.731 versus 0.719), and R-squared is the fairest
> way to compare models with different numbers of predictors. The abdom
> coefficient of 0.95 shows that abdominal circumference causes body fat:
> each extra cm of abdomen adds 0.95 percentage points of fat, so a man who
> reduces his waist by 10 cm will lower his body fat by 9.5 points. One
> record lists a height of 29.5 inches, which is probably a mistake, but I
> kept it in the analysis because more data always improves a regression."

**3.1** This paragraph contains at least four distinct statistical errors.
Identify each one you find (quote the offending phrase), and explain in one
or two sentences why it is wrong. Finding four earns full credit; a fifth
earns a bonus point. (4 pts + 1 bonus)

**3.2** Verify the AI's numbers: report the full model's actual R-squared and
confirm (or refute) the two selected predictor sets and their R-squared
values by running the selections yourself (you did this in 1.2). State which
of the AI's numbers is wrong. (2 pts)
